Degenerative Diseases of the CNS

Neuro · Week 3
LO 1–6 Leading cause of dementia ~5 million Americans Duration 8–10yr

🧠 Alzheimer Disease

▶
▶ Alzheimer's disease - plaques, tangles, causes, symptoms & pathology
Video — "Alzheimer's disease - plaques, tangles, causes, symptoms & pathology" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 74-year-old woman is brought in by her daughter, who reports two years of gradually worsening forgetfulness — first affecting recent conversations and appointments, now increasingly her ability to find words and navigate familiar driving routes. She remains able to dress and bathe herself independently. Neurological exam is nonfocal, and TSH, B12, and RPR are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A degenerative process of the cerebral cortex resulting in senile dementia — the leading cause of dementia in the elderly and the 6th leading cause of death in the US. Synonyms: AD, Alzheimer's dementia, senile dementia of the Alzheimer's type (older term: presenile dementia).

  • ~5 million Americans affected; prevalence ~17 per 1,000 people
  • Incidence and prevalence rise with age; female > male
  • Early-onset (before age 65) familial AD represents ~10% of all AD cases
  • Strongly age-related, with a recognized familial pattern in a subset of cases
Genetics
GeneCharacteristics
APP (chromosome 21)10–15% of early-onset familial AD; trisomy 21 → ↑ risk via APP overexpression; onset age tends to mirror parental onset age (median ~49y)
PSEN1 (presenilin-1)Earliest onset of the familial genes (median ~43y); linked to ~50% of familial AD cases
PSEN2 (presenilin-2)Rarest familial form; latest onset of the three (average ~54y)
APOELate-onset AD risk ↑ with number of ε4 alleles carried; ε2 may be protective; ε3 is neutral

Other risk factors: age ≥65 (strongest predictor for regular/sporadic AD), family history of dementia (strongest predictor for early-onset AD). APP sits on the long arm of chromosome 21, close to the Down syndrome locus; presenilin genes sit on chromosomes 1 and 14. Four susceptibility genes are currently recognized.

Pathophysiology
  • Senile (neuritic) plaques — extracellular, gray matter, composed of Aβ protein. Amyloidogenic pathway (β-secretase → γ-secretase cleavage of APP) generates the neurotoxic Aβ42 fragment, which aggregates into plaques; the nonamyloidogenic pathway (α-secretase → γ-secretase) predominates physiologically and yields nontoxic fragments instead
  • Neurofibrillary tangles — intracellular, composed of hyperphosphorylated tau (an insoluble microtubule-associated protein); tangle burden correlates with degree of cognitive impairment
  • Reduced cholinergic function (degeneration of the nucleus basalis of Meynert)
APP processing — the nonamyloidogenic (α-secretase) pathway predominates normally; the amyloidogenic (β-secretase) pathway generates Aβ42, which aggregates into extracellular plaques
Amyloid plaque and neurofibrillary tangle histology, with their distinct anatomic staging progressions (amyloid: Stage A→B→C; tau/NFT: Stage I/II→III/IV→V/VI) — the two proteinopathies spread through the brain along different paths
Pathology

Macroscopic: diffuse cerebral cortical atrophy with ventriculomegaly, sulcal enlargement, and hippocampal atrophy — most marked in the parietal cortex, with frontal lobe involvement possible. Hippocampal/parahippocampal damage is the earliest gross change; diffuse cortical atrophy and degeneration of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert follow as the disease progresses.

Microscopic: Aβ stains with Congo red under polarization (associated with cerebral amyloid angiopathy); extracellular senile plaques in gray matter; tau neurofibrillary tangles stain with Gallyas silver; Hirano bodies (intracellular rod-shaped eosinophilic actin aggregates, especially in the hippocampus). Neuronal loss concentrates in the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, and neocortical association areas.

Gross specimens — healthy brain (A, B) vs. Alzheimer disease (C, D): significant frontotemporal atrophy (C) and hippocampal atrophy with ventricular expansion (D)
2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation
  • Usually begins in the 7th–9th decade of life; an early-onset form is also recognized
  • Slowly progressive, insidious decline in memory and orientation — episodic (short-term) memory affected first
  • Spreads to language impairment and visuospatial deficits; less commonly, primary progressive aphasia or apraxia
  • Temporal and spatial disorientation
  • Noncognitive/neuropsychiatric symptoms: apathy, agitation/aggression/irritability, depression, urinary incontinence
  • Normal laboratory values are expected
Disease Course

Patients with mild-to-moderate AD often maintain a social facade and preserve certain skills (dressing, hygiene) even as memory declines. ADLs become affected as disease progresses; delusions characterize the later stages. Typical duration is 8–10 years; survival after diagnosis generally ranges 3–10 years.

3 · Diagnostic Workup
History / Physical ExamLabs / Imaging
Diagnosis is based on clinical criteria, often supplemented by formal neuropsychological testingCT/MRI: mainly used to exclude other causes of dementia; may be normal or show nonspecific changes early. Supportive findings if present: generalized/focal atrophy, ventriculomegaly, narrowed gyri, prominent sulci (hydrocephalus ex vacuo), disproportionate medial temporal lobe/hippocampal atrophy
—EEG: nonspecific changes
—PET-CT and CSF analysis (or plasma assays for Aβ and phosphorylated tau) — reserved for diagnostic uncertainty and to guide management, including eligibility for anti-Aβ monoclonal antibody therapy
FDG-PET Pearl

On FDG-PET, AD classically shows hypometabolism in the temporoparietal regions and/or posterior cingulate — a pattern that helps differentiate it from FTD, which instead shows frontal hypometabolism.

FDG-PET (top) and axial FLAIR MRI (bottom) — normal vs. AD (parietal hypometabolism, yellow arrows) vs. FTD (frontal hypometabolism, red arrows)
T2 MRI (vertex level) — bilateral cerebral atrophy with prominent sulci; scattered hyperintense foci reflect enlarged perivascular (Virchow-Robin) spaces
T2 MRI (basal ganglia level) — bilateral cerebral atrophy with prominent Sylvian fissures
T2 MRI (skull base level) — medial temporal lobe atrophy with widened subarachnoid space and dilated temporal horns of the lateral ventricles
4 · Treatment
Pharmacological Treatment

There is currently no curative therapy for AD — all pharmacologic options are modestly effective at slowing symptom progression.

ClassDrug(s)IndicationMechanism
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitorsRivastigmine, Galantamine, DonepezilRivastigmine/Galantamine: mild-moderate; Donepezil: mild-severe↑ ACh at the synapse; AEs include N/V, dizziness/syncope, insomnia, cholinergic crisis, bradycardia/heart block
NMDA receptor antagonistMemantineModerate-severe (often combined with donepezil)↓ glutamate-induced excitotoxicity; AEs: headache, dizziness, confusion, hallucinations, seizures, constipation
Anti-Aβ monoclonal antibodiesLecanemab, DonanemabMild cognitive impairment or mild dementia↓ Aβ plaque formation; AE: ARIA (edema/hemorrhage) — prompt specialist referral needed

Mnemonic for the cholinesterase inhibitors: "Gallantly Down the River" — Galantamine, Donepezil, Rivastigmine.

Adjuncts: antioxidants (very mild effect), anti-inflammatory drugs/statins (still under investigation), SSRIs for concomitant depression, anticonvulsants for concomitant seizures.

5 · Monitoring & Complications
Monitoring & Complications
  • Infections
  • Malnourishment/dehydration
  • Intracerebral hemorrhage — increased risk due to cerebral amyloid angiopathy
  • Family and caregiver support is a core part of ongoing management
6 · Prevention & Health Promotion
Prevention
  • Multidomain lifestyle modification and blood pressure regulation
  • Avoid strong anticholinergic drugs (e.g., diphenhydramine) — heightened impact of adverse effects (confusion, blurred vision, xerostomia) in this population
Pearl

Aβ plaques (extracellular) and tau neurofibrillary tangles (intracellular) follow different anatomic staging patterns as they spread through the brain — part of why plaque burden doesn't correlate with symptom severity as tightly as tangle burden does.

🧩 Frontotemporal Dementia

▶
▶ Frontotemporal Dementia: High Yield Neuro Pathology for the USMLE & COMLEX Exams
Video — "Frontotemporal Dementia: High Yield Neuro Pathology for the USMLE & COMLEX Exams" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 58-year-old man is brought in by his wife, who reports that over the past year he has become increasingly rude to coworkers, started binge-eating sweets he never used to like, and seems unconcerned about missing bill payments. She notes his memory for recent events still seems fairly good. He scores normally on a brief memory screening test but shows poor judgment on tasks requiring planning. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A dementia characterized by early cognitive, behavioral, speech, and motor signs — more prominent than the memory loss seen in Alzheimer disease. FTD represents a cluster of at least three variants (behavioral-variant FTD, primary progressive aphasia, semantic dementia), together termed Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration (FTLD). Older synonym: Pick's disease (now reserved for a specific pathological subtype).

  • 3rd most common cause of cortical dementia, behind Alzheimer disease and Lewy body disease
  • Age of onset typically 40s–60s (some sources cite up to 70) — consistently younger than typical Alzheimer's onset
Etiology & Pathophysiology
  • Majority of cases are sporadic; 20–40% may be linked to an autosomal gene
  • Underlying process: protein malformation and clumping within neurons of the frontal and temporal lobes
  • Associated with pathological intracellular inclusion bodies — Pick bodies (from tau mutations) or progranulin mutations; also associated with ubiquitin inclusion bodies
  • FTLD-tau may be linked to mutations in the MAPT gene (encodes tau protein) — this variant shows tau accumulation without Aβ accumulation, a key molecular distinction from Alzheimer disease (which has both)
Pathology
  • Marked atrophy of the frontal and/or temporal lobes — can be very asymmetric
  • Gliosis and neuronal cell loss
  • Tau or TDP-43 inclusions are found in ~90% of cases; all three clinical variants involve some degree of tau pathology

FTLD-tau (Pick bodies)

  • Round, intracytoplasmic inclusions of aggregated hyperphosphorylated tau

FTLD-TDP

  • Inclusions containing ubiquitinated TDP-43
Gross coronal specimen — marked, asymmetric atrophy of the frontal/temporal cortex with widened sulci, characteristic of frontotemporal lobar degeneration
2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Early symptoms can involve cognitive, behavioral, and sometimes motor abnormalities. Planning and judgment are affected while memory can be relatively spared — global memory, intelligence, and orientation are usually initially preserved, the reverse of typical Alzheimer's.

  • Behavioral changes: apathy, disinhibition (inability to observe social etiquette), weight gain, food fetishes, compulsions, euphoria
  • Late symptoms: motor deficits (e.g. parkinsonism), more widespread cognitive decline

Primary Progressive Aphasia (nonfluent variant)

  • Non-fluent aphasia or mutism
  • Agrammatism
  • Impaired reading and writing
  • Comprehension is intact

Semantic Dementia (semantic variant)

  • Fluent aphasia
  • Anomia
  • Impaired word comprehension
3 · Diagnostic Workup
Diagnostic Approach

Diagnosis is primarily clinical; imaging supports the diagnosis and helps exclude alternative causes rather than confirming it outright.

  • CT/MRI: nonspecific changes — gyral atrophy and sulcal enlargement (sulcomegaly) in the frontal and/or temporal lobes, which can be markedly asymmetric
  • FDG-PET: shows frontal hypometabolism — a pattern that helps distinguish FTD from Alzheimer disease, which instead shows temporoparietal/posterior cingulate hypometabolism
FDG-PET (top) and axial FLAIR MRI (bottom) — normal vs. AD (parietal hypometabolism, yellow arrows) vs. FTD (frontal hypometabolism, red arrows)
Pearl

The fastest way boards distinguish FTD from Alzheimer's: in FTD, personality/behavior change or language impairment comes first while memory stays relatively preserved — in Alzheimer's, episodic memory loss is the presenting symptom.

🕺 Huntington Disease

▶
▶ Huntington disease (Year of the Zebra)
Video — "Huntington disease (Year of the Zebra)" (YouTube)
▶
▶ Section 9.1 Huntington Disease
Video — "Section 9.1 Huntington Disease" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 42-year-old man presents with a 1-year history of involuntary, irregular jerking movements of his arms and face, along with increasing irritability and difficulty concentrating at work. He mentions that his father died in a nursing home in his 60s after years of "strange movements" and dementia. On exam, he has brief, unpredictable, dance-like movements of his limbs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A slowly progressive, autosomal dominant degenerative disease of the basal ganglia with high penetrance, causing combined motor, cognitive, and emotional dysfunction. Synonym: HD.

  • Prevalence ~0.04–0.08 per 1,000 in the US (incidence not well established)
  • Peak incidence ~40 years; typical onset 35–45y (symptom onset can range 20–50y)
  • Equal sex distribution (♀ = ♂)
Etiology & Pathogenesis
  • Mutation in the HTT gene (huntingtin), located on chromosome 4
  • Autosomal dominant inheritance; unstable CAG (polyglutamine) trinucleotide repeats
  • Average repeat number ~19 (normal range 11–34); pathological expression begins at 40 or more repeats
  • Anticipation: CAG repeat number tends to expand further with each generation → progressively earlier onset and more severe disease
  • Polyglutamine repeat proteins interfere with transcription of mitochondrial and antioxidant genes
HTT gene on chromosome 4 — CAG repeat expansion produces a polyglutamine-expanded mutant huntingtin protein that damages the basal ganglia; autosomal dominant inheritance pedigree shown below
Pathophysiology — Circuit Mechanism

Molecular and cellular changes cause neuronal loss and gliosis in the striatum, particularly the caudate nucleus. The striatum normally controls movement via inhibitory outputs along a direct pathway (to globus pallidus internus) and an indirect pathway (to globus pallidus externus):

Early Disease

  • Only the indirect pathway is affected
  • → increased dopaminergic transmission → excess cortical activity → hyperkinetic/choreatic movements

Later Disease

  • Both pathways affected
  • → decreased excitatory thalamocortical transmission → hypokinetic/akinetic symptoms

Neuronal injury/death results from NMDA receptor overactivation via excess glutamate stimulation (excitotoxicity), leading to decreased GABA and decreased acetylcholine in the brain.

Pathology
  • Disease progression typically spans 15–20 years
  • Widespread cerebral atrophy with significant basal ganglia involvement, especially the caudate nucleus
  • Abnormal proteasomal processing of misfolded protein
  • Neuronal cell loss in both cerebral cortex and basal ganglia
2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Insidious onset of chorea with a positive family history is the classic presentation. Behavioral and cognitive disturbances usually accompany the motor disturbance, and progression to dementia occurs.

Symptom progression — initial stages (psychiatric symptoms, hyperkinetic chorea/athetosis, hyperreflexia) vs. advanced stages (cognitive dysfunction, hydrocephalus ex vacuo, hypokinetic bradykinesia/rigidity/dystonia)

Initial Stages

  • Psychiatric: behavioral changes, depression, psychosis
  • Hyperkinetic motor: chorea, athetosis (writhing movements, esp. hands/fingers), hyperreflexia

Advanced Stages

  • Cognitive dysfunction: cognitive decline, dementia
  • Hypokinetic motor: bradykinesia, rigidity, dystonia
  • Major depressive disorder, aggression — psychiatric/behavioral symptoms can mimic substance use
3 · Diagnostic Workup
Diagnostic Approach
  • Genetic testing for the CAG repeat expansion — the definitive diagnostic test
  • CT/MRI: rarely used to make the diagnosis itself, but helps rule out other causes; shows striatal atrophy most pronounced in the caudate nucleus with resulting ex vacuo ventriculomegaly (enlarged, "box-like" frontal horns)
Coronal T1 MRI — enlarged ventricles and subarachnoid space with volume loss of the caudate nuclei (normally convex, here flattened), giving the frontal horns a box-like configuration — hydrocephalus ex vacuo
Normal vs. Huntington disease — schematic comparison showing enlargement of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles as the caudate nucleus atrophies
Pearl

Symptoms flip as HD progresses: early disease is hyperkinetic (chorea, from selective loss of the indirect pathway), while late disease becomes hypokinetic (bradykinesia, rigidity) once the direct pathway is lost too — the mirror image of how Parkinson disease's dopaminergic loss plays out.

👁️ Lewy Body Dementia

▶
▶ Lewy Body Dementia, Causes, Signs and Symptoms, Diagnosis and Treatment
Video — "Lewy Body Dementia, Causes, Signs and Symptoms, Diagnosis and Treatment" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 74-year-old man is brought in by his daughter for evaluation of fluctuating confusion over the past 8 months — some days he is completely lucid, other days he seems markedly disoriented. He has also been seeing "people standing in the corner of the room" that aren't there, and his wife reports he has started acting out his dreams, sometimes kicking her during sleep. On exam he has mild bradykinesia and rigidity, with symptoms having started around the same time as his cognitive changes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A dementia featuring visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, fluctuating alertness, and falls — neuropathologically defined by Lewy bodies throughout the cerebral cortex, amygdala, and substantia nigra. Shares overlapping features with both Alzheimer disease and Parkinson disease. Synonyms: LBD, Lewy body variant of Alzheimer's disease, diffuse Lewy body disease, dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), senile dementia of Lewy body type.

  • Estimates vary by source, but LBD/DLB is generally considered the 2nd most common neurodegenerative dementia after Alzheimer disease (cited ranges: 3–7% of all dementia diagnoses, or as high as 10–15% depending on the source/population)
  • Affects ~1.4 million people in the US
  • 10–15% of Parkinson disease patients will also develop Lewy body-type dementia
  • Male-to-female ratio ~1.5:1 (in contrast to Alzheimer disease, which skews female)
  • Age is the strongest risk factor; most cases occur between 70–85 years
  • Onset ~50–83 years; average survival from diagnosis ~5–7 years
Etiology
  • A disorder of disordered protein dynamics — build-up of α-synuclein in specific CNS neuron groups, disrupting normal function
  • One of several "protein-misfolding diseases," which may arise from overproduction of abnormal protein or breakdown of the normal proteasomal clearance system
  • LBD appears to exist on a spectrum with Parkinson disease
Pathophysiology & Pathology
  • α-Synuclein normally resides in the presynaptic terminal and participates in SNARE complex formation
  • α-Synuclein aggregates to form Lewy bodies — composed of neurofilaments surrounded by amorphous material containing ubiquitin and α-synuclein
  • Lewy bodies are distributed throughout the cerebral cortex, amygdala, cingulate cortex, and substantia nigra
  • Synucleinopathy spectrum: Parkinson disease, Parkinson disease with dementia, and dementia with Lewy bodies; multiple systems atrophy is also related

Macroscopic

  • Cerebral atrophy, particularly of the frontal lobe

Microscopic

  • Lewy bodies — α-synuclein-positive, hyaline cytoplasmic inclusions (especially cortical/subcortical neurons)
  • Lewy neurites — strand-like α-synuclein-containing processes
2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Gradually progressive course; average survival 6–7 years.

  • Cognitive fluctuations — alternating levels of attention and alertness — form a core early feature; can fluctuate rapidly
  • Visual hallucinations (up to 80% of patients)
  • Parkinsonism: parkinsonian-type gait, bradykinesia, rigidity — poor response to levodopa
  • Frequent falls
  • REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) — acting out dreams during sleep
  • Autonomic dysfunction (~90% of patients): orthostatic hypotension, urinary incontinence, constipation, erectile dysfunction, gastroparesis, seborrhea
Presentation Sequence & Treatment Caution

Typical order of symptom onset (percentage reflects how often each symptom is present, not the order itself): memory dysfunction (57%) → visual hallucinations (44%) → depression (34%) → problem-solving difficulties (33%) → gait disturbances (28%) → tremor and stiffness (25%).

Patients have a heightened risk of severe adverse effects from first-generation antipsychotics (including markedly worsened parkinsonism) — yet are more likely to respond well to cholinesterase inhibitors, which can help both cognition and hallucinations.

Pearl — The "1-Year Rule"

The classic way boards distinguish DLB from Parkinson disease dementia (PDD): in DLB, dementia develops within 1 year of motor symptom onset (often together) and is essential to the diagnosis; in PDD, dementia develops years after a well-established Parkinson disease diagnosis — motor symptoms precede cognitive decline by a long interval.

🧠 Practice Questions — Lewy Body Dementia
LO 1–2 α-synucleinopathy — glial, not neuronal Poor levodopa response Survival 7–9yr

🎗️ Multiple System Atrophy

▶
▶ Multiple system atrophy (MSA) (Year of the Zebra 2025)
Video — "Multiple system atrophy (MSA) (Year of the Zebra 2025)" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 58-year-old man presents with a 1-year history of progressive imbalance and slurred speech, along with new lightheadedness on standing that has led to several falls. He also reports erectile dysfunction and urinary urgency. On exam he has a wide-based, ataxic gait, mild bradykinesia, and a significant drop in blood pressure on standing. A trial of levodopa produced minimal improvement in his motor symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A group of neurodegenerative diseases that can involve multiple areas of the brain and the autonomic nervous system, divided by predominant presentation:

  • MSA-P — presents as parkinsonism
  • MSA-C — presents as olivopontocerebellar atrophy (cerebellar-predominant)
  • MSA-A — presents with autonomic dysfunction, once termed Shy-Drager syndrome
  • Incidence in individuals >50yo ~3/100,000 (some sources cite 1–3/100,000/year overall); prevalence ~2–5/100,000
  • Mean age of onset ~54–56 years
  • Male-to-female ratio uncertain
  • Mean survival 7–9 years
Etiology, Pathogenesis & Pathology

A form of misfolded protein disease — an α-synucleinopathy. Uniquely among the synucleinopathies, α-synuclein aggregates primarily in oligodendrocytes (glial cells) rather than neurons, forming glial cytoplasmic inclusions (GCIs) — contrast with Parkinson disease and DLB, where α-synuclein instead aggregates in neurons as Lewy bodies.

α-synuclein aggregates in oligodendrocytes (GCIs)
→
Oligodendrocyte dysfunction & demyelination
→
Neuronal loss and gliosis
  • Cerebellar form: atrophy of the cerebellum, basis pontis, and inferior olive
  • Atrophy of the substantia nigra and putamen
  • Autonomic form: loss of catecholaminergic brainstem nuclei and the intermediolateral nucleus of the thoracic spinal cord
  • Broader microscopic picture: gliosis, axonal degeneration, and glial/neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, putamen, locus ceruleus, pontine nuclei, cerebellum, and inferior olivary nuclei
The three affected systems — parkinsonism (substantia nigra/putamen/globus pallidus), cerebellar dysfunction (cerebellum/peduncle/pons), and autonomic dysfunction (intermediolateral spinal column/Onuf nucleus/medulla) — with the underlying glial α-synuclein mechanism below
Imaging Correlates

Although not a formally tested diagnostic step at this LO level, imaging directly visualizes the pathology above:

Serial MRI — sagittal T1 (A, D) and axial T2 (B/C, E/F) at baseline vs. 2 years later, showing progressive atrophy of the cerebellum, pons, midbrain, and middle cerebellar peduncle
FDG-PET — mild hypometabolism in the posterior parietal lobes (A) and posterior cingulate (D), with markedly decreased uptake in the basal ganglia and cerebellum (B, C)
Axial T2/FLAIR — cerebellar and pontine signal change; the classic cross-shaped pontine hyperintensity ("hot cross bun sign") reflects selective degeneration of the transverse pontocerebellar tracts and median pontine raphe — relatively specific for MSA-C, though not pathognomonic (also described in variant CJD, pontine infarction, and corticobasal degeneration)

Emerging research is also exploring biomarkers beyond imaging — α-synuclein and related markers (NfL, GFAP) in CSF, blood, skin, olfactory mucosa, and even gut microbiota are being studied as potential future diagnostic tools.

Emerging biomarker research — potential diagnostic markers under investigation across imaging, CSF, blood, skin, olfactory mucosa/saliva, and gut microbiota
2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Atypical parkinsonism in combination with cerebellar ataxia and autonomic dysfunction — three distinct neuroanatomical circuits are involved:

Striatonigral System

  • Parkinsonism: bradykinesia, rigidity, postural instability, tremor
  • Poor response to levodopa

Olivopontocerebellar System

  • Gait/limb ataxia, dysarthria, dysmetria, nystagmus

Autonomic Nervous System

  • Orthostatic hypotension, urogenital dysfunction, GI dysfunction, sweating abnormalities
  • Sleep and breathing disorders (e.g. REM sleep behavior disorder)
  • Cognitive function can be relatively normal — a useful distinguishing point from DLB/Parkinson disease dementia
  • Pyramidal signs possible (e.g. unexplained extensor plantar reflex); speech impairment including croaky voice from laryngeal dystonia
  • Classified as MSA-C or MSA-P based on the predominant feature at initial presentation
Pearls

Poor levodopa response plus ataxia and/or early, severe autonomic failure should shift your differential away from idiopathic Parkinson disease and toward MSA.

MSA is the one synucleinopathy with glial (not neuronal) α-synuclein pathology — a high-yield distinguishing point from Parkinson disease and DLB.

🧓 Parkinson Disease

▶
▶ Parkinson disease - physiology, pathology, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, treatment
Video — "Parkinson disease - physiology, pathology, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, treatment" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 61-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of a resting tremor in his right hand that improves with voluntary movement, along with a sensation of stiffness in his right arm. His wife has noticed he blinks less often and his handwriting has become progressively smaller. On exam he has cogwheel rigidity of the right upper extremity and a slow, shuffling gait with reduced arm swing on the right. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A slowly progressive, degenerative disease of the substantia nigra and the nigrostriatal fibers of the basal ganglia — one of a growing class of disorders involving abnormal α-synuclein deposition. Synonyms: PD, paralysis agitans, shaking palsy.

  • The 2nd most common neurodegenerative disease overall, and the most common familial neurodegenerative disease
  • Incidence rises with age: rare before 45, reaching 1–2/1,000 in those >65; most common onset 45–65y (peak age cited as 50–60y in some sources); prevalence in >65y ~0.7/1,000
  • Equal sex distribution; occurs across all ethnic groups at roughly equal frequency
  • Risk factors: positive family history, male gender, head injury, pesticide exposure, well water consumption, rural living
Pathology
  • Mild atrophy of the frontal lobes
  • Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra — grossly visible as loss of the normal pigmented (neuromelanin-containing) cells
  • Lewy bodies present in the remaining dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra, containing α-synuclein — a chaperone protein normally unique to the brain and involved in SNARE complex formation
  • Oxidative stress appears to be a key factor driving neuronal loss
Substantia nigra, gross specimen — Parkinson disease (left) vs. normal (right); note the loss of pigmented (neuromelanin-containing) cells in the parkinsonian specimen
α-Synuclein immunostaining — spherical intracytoplasmic Lewy bodies and strand-like Lewy neurites in substantia nigra neurons
A: H&E — an eosinophilic Lewy body inside a neuron, alongside abundant neuromelanin granules. B: α-synuclein immunostain highlighting a Lewy neurite

PD sits on the same synucleinopathy spectrum as dementia with Lewy bodies — the key distinction is largely topographic: PD's pathology concentrates in the substantia nigra, while DLB's Lewy bodies are diffusely distributed through the cortex.

2 · Clinical Presentation
Cardinal Manifestations — TRAP
  • Tremor — resting, 4–6 Hz
  • Rigidity — cogwheel or lead-pipe
  • Akinesia/bradykinesia
  • Postural instability

Slow progressive course with unilateral onset progressing to bilateral distribution. Onset can also feature weakness, fatigue, incoordination, and aching/discomfort.

Clinical features — stooped posture, reduced arm swing, festinating shuffling gait, hypomimia/seborrhea, and tremor with micrographia

Other Motor Manifestations

  • Masked facies (hypomimia); decreased blink reflex
  • Stooped posture; shuffling and festinating gait
  • Decreased associated movements (arm swing) with gait

Non-Motor Manifestations

  • Depression and anxiety; cognitive impairment
  • Sleep disturbance; achy pain; autonomic disturbances
  • Early symptoms can include hyposmia and constipation
3 · Diagnostic Workup
Diagnostic Approach
  • History and physical exam — PD remains primarily a clinical diagnosis
  • Imaging can assist in ruling out associated or alternative diseases, but is not required to make the diagnosis
4 · Treatment
Pharmacological Treatment

Goal: maintain function and quality of life.

Dopaminergic synapse — mechanism of action for each drug class, from precursor (L-DOPA) through receptor agonists, enzyme inhibitors, and adjunct anticholinergic/NMDA-antagonist therapy
ClassExample(s)Mechanism
Dopamine precursorL-DOPA (levodopa)Converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase at the presynaptic neuron
Decarboxylase inhibitorCarbidopaBlocks peripheral L-DOPA→dopamine conversion; can't cross the BBB, so no central effect/side effects — reduces peripheral side effects of levodopa
Dopamine agonistsRopinirole (nonergot), bromocriptine (ergot)Directly bind and stimulate the dopamine receptor
COMT inhibitorsEntacapone (peripheral), tolcapone (central + peripheral)↓ dopamine metabolism → decreased L-DOPA demand, longer effect per dose
MAO-B inhibitorsSelegiline↓ central dopamine breakdown → prolonged effect
AnticholinergicsBenztropine↓ relative excitatory acetylcholine tone versus dopamine
NMDA antagonistsAmantadineGlutamate NMDA receptor antagonism → dopaminergic effect
Surgical & Other Treatment
  • Deep brain stimulation (DBS) — modern surgical option, alongside older ablative techniques (pallidotomy, thalamotomy); typically reserved for patients with disabling motor fluctuations despite optimized medical therapy
  • Neurotransplantation of fetal catecholaminergic cells (experimental/historical)
Skull X-ray — bilateral deep brain stimulation electrodes with leads coursing to a subcutaneous pulse generator connection
5 · Monitoring & Complications
Monitoring & Complications
  • Ongoing therapy needed for non-motor symptoms — behavioral issues, dementia
  • Drug-induced dyskinesia from long-term levodopa therapy
  • On-off phenomenon — unpredictable swings between mobility and immobility with long-term drug use
  • Life expectancy is normal with treatment, but patients often become dependent on care in later stages
Pearl

Carbidopa's inability to cross the blood-brain barrier is exactly what makes it useful — it blocks only the peripheral conversion of levodopa, leaving more intact levodopa to reach the brain for central conversion to dopamine.

🧠 Practice Questions — Parkinson Disease
LO 1–4 2nd most common dementia (US/EU) Ischemic or hemorrhagic No licensed treatment

🩸 Vascular Dementia

▶
▶ Vascular dementia - causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, pathology
Video — "Vascular dementia - causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, pathology" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 72-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and two prior strokes is brought in by her family, who report that her thinking and memory declined in a series of noticeable drops over the past three years, with long stable periods in between rather than a smooth decline. She also has a mildly unsteady gait and occasional word-finding difficulty. MRI shows multiple old lacunar infarcts and periventricular white matter changes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

Dementia resulting from ischemic or hemorrhagic tissue injury in brain regions that translates into cognitive impairment — injury may involve localized large-vessel disease or diffuse small-vessel disease. (There is a growing conceptual movement to consider Alzheimer disease itself as a possible diffuse small-vessel vascular dementia.) Synonyms: arteriosclerotic dementia, hypertensive encephalopathy.

  • 2nd most common cause of dementia in the US and Europe — but the most common form in parts of Asia
  • Prevalence ~1.5% in Western countries; ~2.2% in Japan
  • Prevalence increases with age
Etiology — Recognized Forms
  • Multi-infarct dementia — embolic showers producing multiple cortical infarcts
  • Small vessel dementia — lacunes, extensive white matter lesions, infarcts, demyelination, gliosis; includes Binswanger disease (subcortical vascular dementia)
  • Strategic infarct dementia — infarcts in strategic locations (e.g. the thalamus)
  • Hemorrhagic dementia — hemorrhagic changes, may be associated with cerebral amyloid angiopathy
  • Hereditary vascular dementia (CADASIL) — multiple lacunes and white matter lesions, classically affecting temporal lobe white matter; caused by a mutation in the NOTCH3 gene
  • Alzheimer disease with cardiovascular complications — combined vascular changes and atrophy

Underlying mechanisms (per Amboss): large artery occlusion (cortical ischemia), lacunar infarcts (small vessel occlusion, subcortical ischemia), and chronic subcortical ischemia.

Risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, age, stroke, genetic factors) feeding into three symptom domains: behavioral, locomotor, and executive dysfunction

Leucoaraiosis: a purely radiographic term describing numerous hyperintense white matter lesions on T2-weighted MRI in elderly individuals — suggestive of underlying cerebrovascular disease such as multi-infarct dementia.

2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Progressive cognitive impairment, slowing of movement and reaction time, and memory loss.

Multi-Infarct / Poststroke Pattern

  • Step-wise deterioration — sudden drops with intervening stable periods

Diffuse Small-Vessel / CADASIL Pattern

  • Gradual, progressive decline
  • Subcortical features: reduced executive function, memory loss, mood disorders (depression), behavioral changes (apathy)
  • Other: motor deterioration, dysphagia, dysarthria, gait disturbance, autonomic dysfunction
3 · Diagnostic Testing
Diagnostic Approach
  • Imaging — typically MRI and CT; MRA/CTA when available
  • MRI findings: multiple cortical infarcts, subcortical (lacunar) infarcts, white matter lesions (periventricular and semioval center)
  • CT findings: microangiopathic white matter lesions, multiple subcortical lacunar infarcts
  • Specialized genetic testing available for CADASIL
  • Differential diagnoses: other dementia subtypes (e.g. Alzheimer disease), metabolic/endocrine causes (B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism), infections (e.g. neurosyphilis)
Noncontrast CT — low-attenuation zones in the periventricular white matter adjacent to the frontal and temporal horns, with prominent sulci and ventricles
Noncontrast CT — periventricular white matter low attenuation with two frontal lacunar infarcts
T2-weighted MRI — enlarged ventricles with periventricular white matter signal change
Spectrum of small-vessel disease on MRI — white matter lesions ranging from punctate foci to extensive confluent abnormalities, with lacunar infarcts
4 · Treatment
Treatment
  • There are currently no efficacious or licensed treatments for vascular dementia itself
  • Focus on the underlying causes: hypertension, atherosclerosis, diabetes mellitus
  • Antiplatelet drugs to help prevent further cerebrovascular damage
  • Supportive care
Pearl

Stepwise, fluctuating decline is the classic clue for multi-infarct vascular dementia versus Alzheimer's smooth insidious course — but small-vessel/Binswanger-type vascular dementia can look just as gradual as Alzheimer's, so imaging and vascular risk factors still do the real distinguishing work.

🧠 Practice Questions — Vascular Dementia
LO 1–4 Combined UMN + LMN Median survival 3–5yr Lou Gehrig's Disease

⚡ Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis

▶
▶ Understanding Motor Neurone Disease (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis)
Video — "Understanding Motor Neurone Disease (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis)" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 63-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive weakness and cramping in his right hand, which has spread to the right arm and, more recently, the left hand. On examination he has muscle atrophy and fasciculations of the intrinsic hand muscles bilaterally, along with hyperreflexia and a positive Babinski sign in the lower extremities. Extraocular movements are full, and sensory examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

An unrelentingly progressive degenerative disease of neurons in the peripheral and central motor systems — also known as motor neuron disease or Lou Gehrig's Disease. Some variants also include degenerative changes in the frontal and temporal lobes.

  • Incidence ~0.01/1,000 persons; prevalence remains low because of the disease's rapid lethality (~1.5/100,000 people)
  • The most common form of progressive motor neuron disease
  • Mean age of onset ~65 years
  • Median survival ~3–5 years after symptom onset; only 10–20% survive to 10 years
Overview infographic — background, causes, signs/symptoms, diagnosis, and treatment at a glance
Etiology & Pathogenesis
  • Most cases are idiopathic (sporadic); familial ALS has a genetic background — SOD1 (superoxide dismutase), C9orf72, and TDP-43 mutations are implicated
  • Risk factors: prolonged heavy metal exposure, smoking, military service
  • Contributing mechanisms: oxidative stress, excitotoxicity, mitochondrial and proteasomal dysfunction
Astrocyte failure to clear synaptic glutamate
→
Continual motor neuron activation
→
Excitotoxicity + oxidative stress
→
SOD enzyme failure
→
Motor neuron death
Pathology
  • Hallmark: death of peripheral motor neurons (ventral horn, brainstem nuclei) and central motor neurons (bulbospinal, corticospinal) — combined UMN + LMN degeneration at two or more levels
  • CN III, IV, VI are classically spared — extraocular movements stay full even late in disease
  • Denervation of skeletal muscle → weakness and atrophy
  • Peripheral and central sensory systems remain unaffected; autonomic function is generally intact (though dysautonomia can appear as a late feature)
  • Death usually from respiratory failure; average survival from diagnosis is 3–5 years
UMN pathway from motor cortex through the medulla to bulbar and limb lower motor neurons — the two levels of degeneration that together define ALS
2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation
  • Onset often asymmetric — typically one hand — progressing to symmetric involvement
  • Early muscle cramping, often noticed in the morning while stretching in bed
  • Spinal (LMN) involvement: flaccid weakness, atrophy, fasciculations
  • Corticospinal (UMN) involvement: spastic weakness
  • Bulbar involvement (~25% at onset): dysphagia, dysarthria, dyspnea — eventually leading to aspiration; pseudobulbar palsy with pseudobulbar affect can occur
  • Fasciculations, spasticity, clonus
Normal vs. ALS-affected motor neuron — once the connecting motor neuron degenerates, the voluntary muscle it innervates can no longer contract
Clinical progression — muscle weakness, dysarthria, and eventual respiratory compromise, alongside the healthy-vs-damaged motor neuron comparison
Late Features

Dementia is not a normal part of core ALS progression, but ~15% of patients develop frontotemporal dementia as part of the ALS-FTD spectrum. Other late features: dysautonomia (constipation, neurogenic bladder), respiratory muscle weakness/failure, severe dysphagia.

3 · Diagnostic Workup
History / Physical ExamLabs / Electrodiagnostics
Complete neurological exam; diagnosis is one of exclusion — must rule out other motor system diseases (multifocal motor neuropathy, myasthenia gravis, LEMS, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, thyrotoxicosis, poliomyelitis)Nerve conduction studies: sensory and motor conduction usually normal
Definitive diagnostic criteria require evidence of UMN + LMN involvement across bulbar, cervical, thoracic, and lumbar regionsEMG: fibrillations and positive sharp waves (denervation)
—Labs: ↑↑ creatine kinase (CK); rule out Lyme disease and heavy metal poisoning
4 · Treatment
Treatment

Disease-Modifying Agents

  • Riluzole — sodium channel blocker, inhibits CNS glutamate release/excitotoxicity; prolongs life ~2–3 months on average, slows functional decline in late-stage disease
  • Edaravone — reactive oxygen species scavenger; slows functional decline in some patients
  • Tofersen — antisense oligonucleotide blocking expression of the defective SOD1 gene; remarkable success halting progression in SOD1-mutation-positive patients specifically, with some evidence of pathology reversal enabling rehabilitation

Symptomatic & Supportive

  • Symptom management: quinine or muscle relaxants for cramps/spasticity
  • Multidisciplinary care: nursing, physiotherapy, eventual respiratory support and enteral feeding
Pearls

CN III, IV, VI sparing is a classic bedside clue — full extraocular movements even in advanced ALS point away from other diffuse motor/neuromuscular syndromes.

Mnemonic: "Riluzole rilly helps treat Lou Gehrig disease."

🧠 Practice Questions — Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
LO 1–3 Autosomal recessive SMN1/SMN2, chromosome 5 Non-sitters / Sitters / Walkers

👶 Spinal Muscular Atrophy

📺 Supplementary resource: Osmosis — Spinal Muscular Atrophy
🎯 How boards would word it

A 4-month-old girl is brought in for evaluation of progressive weakness. Her mother reports she has never held her head up well and now seems even floppier than before. On exam she has severe hypotonia, symmetric weakness of the legs greater than the arms, tongue fasciculations, and absent deep tendon reflexes. Her eye movements are full, and she is cognitively alert and interactive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A progressive neuromuscular disorder resulting in degeneration of α-motoneurons (lower motor neurons) in the ventral horn of the spinal cord. Beginning in the fetus, these diseases eventually cause extensive motoneuron death with resultant muscle denervation and atrophy.

  • Incidence estimates range ~1 in 6,000–11,000 live births (4–10 per 100,000); prevalence ~1–2/100,000
  • SMN1 carrier frequency ~1 in 40
  • Most forms are autosomal recessive; some sources note a slight male predominance
  • Historically considered a childhood disease, but increasingly seen in adults thanks to improved supportive care and newer therapies
Etiology & Pathophysiology
  • The Survival Motor Neuron (SMN) gene is required for motor neuron survival — a ribosome-associated factor involved in translation. Two similar copies sit on chromosome 5: SMN1 (telomeric) and SMN2 (centromeric)
  • SMN1 normally produces all the functional SMN protein needed
  • SMN2 differs from SMN1 by loss of exon 7 — its protein product is only partially functional and degrades rapidly
  • When SMN1 is defective, residual SMN2 copy number can blunt disease severity (up to ~5 copies) — more copies of the partially-functional gene, milder phenotype (though SMN2 copy number is variable and not perfectly correlated with phenotype)
  • Molecular cascade: SMN1 defect → defective snRNP assembly (SMN complex) → apoptosis of lower motor neurons (especially anterior horn cells) in late fetal development/postnatal period
Pathology

SMA reflects the pathological continuation of a normal developmental process — programmed motor neuron cell death that is a normal part of embryonic life becomes excessive and persists pathologically.

Selective vulnerability: only lower motor neurons (spinal ± bulbar) are affected. Sensation is not affected. Motor neurons of CN III, IV, and VI and sacral motor neurons are spared — preserving eye movements and continence, even in severe disease.

2 · Clinical Presentation
General Presentation

Progressive, symmetric, proximal-predominant muscle weakness and atrophy — earlier onset means more severe disease. Legs are often more affected than arms, though axial, intercostal, and bulbar muscles can be involved. Classic infant presentation: frog-leg posture, weak cry, difficulty sitting/rolling, and increased respiratory effort with paradoxical breathing. Intellectual disability is rare.

Mnemonic: Type 1 = non-sitters, Type 2 = sitters, Type 3 = walkers — the later the onset, the better the prognosis.

TypeOnsetMotor MilestoneLife Expectancy
0PrenatalNone achieved; severe hypotonia, respiratory distress, cannot suck/swallow, cardiac abnormalitiesWeeks–months
1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann)<6 monthsNon-sitter — severe hypotonia, tongue fasciculations, bell-shaped thorax/belly breathing, bulbar involvement<2 years
26–18 monthsSitter — can sit unsupported but cannot stand/walk; scoliosis develops long-term; minimal bulbar involvement~3rd decade
3 (Kugelberg-Welander)>18 monthsWalker — can sit, stand, and ambulate alone; no bulbar symptomsNormal
410–30 years (adult)Stands and walks; mild phenotypeNormal
Spine X-ray — scoliosis in SMA type II, a long-term musculoskeletal complication in patients who survive with sitting-level function but progressive axial weakness
Classification of SMA by SMN2 copy number — note type III is further split into IIIa (onset 18mo–3yr) and IIIb (onset >3yr); SMN2 copy number is highly variable and not tightly correlated to phenotype, but these reflect the most common pattern per subtype (Rad, Cai & Weiss, Muscle Nerve 2022)
3 · Diagnostic Testing
Diagnostic Approach
  • Genetic testing for the SMN1 mutation/deletion — best initial and confirmatory test
  • Muscle biopsy: atrophy of groups of motor units interspersed with normal or hypertrophied motor units ("grouped atrophy")
  • EMG: spontaneous, large-amplitude, low-frequency electrical activity (rarified interference pattern) — a denervation pattern
  • Labs: creatine kinase (CK) normal or only mildly elevated — a useful contrast to muscular dystrophies, where CK is markedly elevated
  • MRI: muscle atrophy pattern varies with severity (fatty infiltration in mild forms, ragged atrophy in intermediate, gross atrophy in severe); spinal cord may show atrophy and T2 hyperintensity in the anterior horns of the cervical cord (the "owl's eyes" appearance)
Differential Diagnosis

Congenital myasthenic syndromes (fatigable weakness, ptosis, extraocular involvement), congenital myopathies, viral infections like polio/coxsackievirus/echovirus/West Nile (acute, ascending flaccid paralysis), hypotonic cerebral palsy (non-progressive), muscular dystrophies (markedly ↑↑ CK), juvenile ALS (predominantly bulbar), and progressive muscular atrophy (nonhereditary, adult-onset).

Pearl

SMA spares three things many other severe infantile neuromuscular diseases don't: sensation, extraocular movements, and continence — a useful triad for excluding mimics at the bedside.

Recent Therapeutic Advances (context)

Although beyond this LO's core scope, three newer therapies have transformed SMA management: nusinersen (antisense oligonucleotide altering SMN2 splicing to produce functional protein; requires annual intrathecal injection), risdiplam (oral mRNA splicing modulator, same target as nusinersen but taken by mouth), and onasemnogene abeparvovec / Zolgensma (AAV9-vector gene therapy delivering a functional SMN1 copy, given once intravenously).

🧠 Practice Questions — Spinal Muscular Atrophy
LO 1–2 Spasticity > weakness >50 genetic types Normal life expectancy

🦵 Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia

🎯 How boards would word it

A 34-year-old man presents with several years of progressive stiffness and difficulty walking, describing his gait as feeling like his legs are "scissoring." He also reports occasional urinary urgency. His father had similar symptoms starting in his 30s. On exam he has increased tone and hyperreflexia in both legs with bilateral Babinski signs, but strength is only mildly reduced, and vibration sense is minimally diminished. Cognition is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A group of rare genetic disorders involving degenerative myelopathy of the axons innervating the lower-extremity corticospinal fibers — >50 genetic types identified (over 87 loci by some counts). Divided into two major categories:

  • Uncomplicated (pure): involves only corticospinal axons — the most common form; autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked variants all recognized
  • Complicated: involves corticospinal axons plus dorsal column and spinocerebellar tract axons
  • Very rare — one Ireland-based study found a prevalence of 1.27 per 10,000; other estimates cite incidence <10 per 100,000
  • Age of onset is highly variable — from early childhood to the 8th decade of life
Etiology & Pathogenesis
  • Genetic defect: autosomal dominant (most common), autosomal recessive, X-linked, or sporadic mutations
  • Example subtype — HSP56: autosomal recessive, caused by a mutation in CYP2U1 (cytochrome P450 2U1, involved in fatty acid metabolism and neurologic function); classified as complicated due to associated peripheral neuropathy, intellectual disability, and extrapyramidal symptoms
  • Core mechanism: defects in genes required for normal (fast) axonal neurotransmission → degeneration mainly of the longest axons in the CNS
  • Length-dependent, retrograde ("dying-back") degeneration — explains why the corticospinal tract fibers to the lower extremities (the longest CNS axons) are hit earliest and hardest
Pathology

Dying-back myelopathy, with degeneration in both crossed and uncrossed corticospinal fibers. In complicated forms, degeneration extends to the dorsal columns and spinocerebellar tracts as well.

2 · Clinical Presentation
Pure (Uncomplicated) HSP

Insidious onset, slow progression, symmetric or near-symmetric lower extremity spasticity more than weakness:

  • Upper motor neuron paralysis of bilateral lower limbs; increased extensor tone; spasticity/hypertonicity → contractures
  • Gait abnormalities: delayed walking initiation (childhood-onset) or scissoring gait (late-onset)
  • Brisk deep tendon reflexes; extensor plantar reflex (Babinski sign)
  • Dorsal column dysfunction — usually mild, often only detected on exam (↓ vibration sense, 2-point discrimination, position sense)
  • Urinary urgency and urge incontinence
  • High-arch feet, hammer-toe deformity; atrophy of lower extremity muscles
Complicated HSP

All the features of pure HSP plus additional neurological findings, which vary by genetic subtype:

  • Epilepsy/seizures, intellectual disability, dementia (associated with corpus callosum thinning in some forms)
  • Cerebellar or extrapyramidal signs: ataxia, nystagmus
  • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Vision/hearing loss: deafness, cataracts, ophthalmoparesis, retinal pigmentary degeneration, optic atrophy
Prognosis by Onset

HSP may be nonprogressive (childhood-onset — most patients remain ambulant) or progressive (adult-onset — often wheelchair-bound by ~age 70). Life expectancy is normal regardless of onset age.

Pearl

The hallmark clue for HSP is spasticity out of proportion to weakness — prominent upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski, increased tone) with relatively preserved strength, unlike primary lower motor neuron or muscle weakness disorders.

Management Context

Beyond this LO's core scope: there is no cure for HSP. Management is supportive — muscle relaxants or botulinum toxin for spasticity, anticholinergics (e.g. oxybutynin) for urinary urgency, physiotherapy to prevent contractures, and orthotic devices. Surgical options (selective dorsal rhizotomy, intrathecal baclofen) are reserved for severe, refractory spasticity.

Management overview — physiotherapy (electrical stimulation, robotic gait training, hydrotherapy), pharmaceutical options in current use and under investigation, and surgical intervention (selective dorsal rhizotomy, intrathecal baclofen) for refractory spasticity
🧠 Practice Questions — Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia
LO 1–2 ~60 forms described Mostly autosomal dominant CAG repeat / polyglutamine

🎯 Spinocerebellar Ataxias

▶
▶ Spinocerebellar Ataxia | Pathology, diagnosis and treatment | USMLE
Video — "Spinocerebellar Ataxia | Pathology, diagnosis and treatment of Spinocerebellar Ataxia | USMLE" (YouTube)
▶
▶ Spinocerebellar Ataxia (NORD)
Video — "Spinocerebellar Ataxia (NORD)" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 38-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of progressive unsteadiness while walking and slurred speech. His father and paternal grandmother had similar symptoms beginning in their 40s, with each successive generation seeming to develop symptoms earlier and more severely. On exam he has a wide-based gait, dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing, nystagmus, and scanning speech. Strength and reflexes are preserved, and cognition is intact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A complex, heterogeneous group of hereditary degenerative disorders unified by progressively worsening ataxia. Degeneration typically centers on the cerebellum and its connections, but can also involve the spinal cord, brainstem, and peripheral nerve. ~60 forms described (some sources cite >30 confirmed types); ~40 share a common autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and are designated SCA + a number reflecting order of mutation discovery (also called ADCA — autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxias). Recessive (SCAR) and X-linked (SCAX) forms are also documented.

Synonyms: progressive ataxias, hereditary ataxias, autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxias. Nota bene: SCA1 was originally named olivopontocerebellar atrophy; SCA3 was originally Machado-Joseph disease.

  • ADCA prevalence ~1–9 per 100,000 worldwide; age of onset typically 30–55 years
  • Gene distributions vary significantly by geography and ethnicity
  • SCA3 (Machado-Joseph disease) is the most common progressive ataxia worldwide — it arose independently in Asia and in Portugal, with the Portuguese variant spreading globally via emigration
Cross-Reference

The single most common inherited ataxia overall is actually autosomal recessive — Friedreich ataxia — which retains its own distinct name and is covered separately.

Etiology & Pathophysiology
  • Influenced by >50 different genes across >48 loci; most (but not all) forms are autosomal dominant
  • Mutations cluster into three general groups: polyglutamine disorders, channelopathies (calcium or potassium channels), and gene expression disorders
  • The most common SCAs (SCA1–3, SCA6, SCA7, SCA17) are polyglutamine disorders caused by CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the corresponding ataxin genes — regulatory genes involved in transcription and clearance of damaged protein
  • Repeats are unstable and tend to expand further in successive generations — the same anticipation phenomenon seen in Huntington disease
  • SCA1 example: locus on chromosome 6; mutant allele has 40–83 CAG repeats vs. 6–39 in the normal allele
  • SCA2 (chromosome 12, ataxin-2) and SCA3 (chromosome 14, ataxin-3) are two other major loci
Pathology

Degenerative changes center on the cerebellum and its associated pathways. Depending on the specific variant, degeneration can extend to the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, spinal cord, peripheral nerves, retina, and optic nerve.

ADCA TypeExample SCAsAdditional Features Beyond Ataxia
Type ISCA1–4, SCA8, SCA10, SCA12–23, SCA25, SCA27, SCA28Optic atrophy, extraocular muscle paralysis, dementia, extrapyramidal symptoms
Type IISCA7Pigmentary maculopathy → blindness
Type IIISCA5, SCA6, SCA11, SCA26, SCA29–31Ataxia only; usually late onset
2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Presentation varies widely by mutation type, but all forms involve ataxia.

  • Progressively worsening, symmetric limb ataxia — the dominant finding
  • Impairment of gait (usually broad-based) and equilibrium
  • Slowness of voluntary movements
  • Some sensory system impairment present in most forms
  • Scanning speech and dysarthria
  • Nystagmoid eye movements (nystagmus)
  • Tremor of the neck and head
  • Dyssynergia, dysmetria, and/or dysdiadochokinesia may be present

Most patients retain full mental capacity while progressively developing severe, irreversible disability within ~15 years of symptom onset (though Type I ADCA forms can include dementia as an exception).

Pearl

Like Huntington disease, most SCAs are triggered by unstable CAG repeat expansion causing a polyglutamine disease — and just like HD, repeat length tends to grow across generations (anticipation), producing earlier and more severe disease with each successive generation.

🧠 Practice Questions — Spinocerebellar Ataxias
LO 1–3 Most common hereditary ataxia Autosomal recessive, GAA repeat Cardiomyopathy = #1 cause of death

🫀 Friedreich Ataxia

▶
▶ What is Friedreich's Ataxia? Causes, Symptoms & Inheritance
Video — "What is Friedreich's Ataxia? Causes, Symptoms & Inheritance" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 14-year-old girl is brought in for evaluation of progressive clumsiness and frequent falls over the past 2 years. Her parents note she has difficulty with fine motor tasks and her speech has become slurred. On exam she has a wide-based, staggering gait, absent deep tendon reflexes throughout, extensor plantar responses bilaterally, loss of vibration and position sense in the feet, and pes cavus deformity. Echocardiogram shows concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

The classic form of progressive hereditary spinocerebellar ataxia and the most common form of hereditary ataxia overall. Involves a mutation in the frataxin (FXN) gene on chromosome 9q13, with significant loss of myelinated fibers in the posterior columns, spinocerebellar tracts, and corticospinal tracts of the spinal cord.

  • Incidence ~1 in 50,000 in the US (~3–4 per 100,000 by other estimates)
  • Peak incidence age 8–15 years; most cases present before age 25
  • Male > female; most common in individuals of Central and Northern European descent
Etiology & Pathogenesis
  • Autosomal recessive — GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in intron 1 of the FXN gene, chromosome 9q13-q21.1 → decreased frataxin protein expression
  • Frataxin normally resides on the inner mitochondrial membrane and participates in iron-sulfur cluster formation for mitochondrial complexes I and II
GAA repeat expansion
→
Absent/deficient frataxin
→
Impaired mitochondrial Fe-S cluster formation
→
Free ionic iron accumulation + ↓ATP
→
Oxidative damage → cell death

Most vulnerable cell types: neurons, cardiac myocytes, and pancreatic cells — the highest energy-demand tissues.

Cellular mechanism — GAA repeat expansion → absent frataxin → impaired mitochondrial iron handling → free radical formation and reduced ATP → oxidative damage and cell death, with neurons, cardiac cells, and pancreatic cells most affected
Pathology
  • Progressive myelin and axon loss, in order of severity: spinocerebellar tracts > posterior columns > corticospinal tracts
  • Fibrous gliosis present in these tracts
  • Reduced neurons in the nucleus of Clarke's column and dorsal root ganglia (lumbosacral > cervical)
  • Cell loss also in the dentate nucleus of the cerebellum and inferior olivary nucleus of the medulla; Purkinje cell loss in the cerebellar cortex
Tract-symptom correlation — spinocerebellar tracts (ataxia), dorsal columns and dorsal root ganglia (loss of proprioception/vibration sense), and lateral corticospinal tract (spastic weakness)

Mnemonic: "FRiedreich ATAXia → ATAXic GAAit → GAA repeat in the FRATAXin gene."

2 · Clinical Presentation
Cardinal Manifestations
  • Presents before age 25; initial complaint is typically difficulty walking from ataxia
  • Progressive limb and gait ataxia, lower extremities >> upper extremities; progressively worsening staggering gait with falls; titubations
  • Both sensory and cerebellar ataxia present in gait — widespread unstable stance with constantly shifting position, foot slapping
  • Romberg sign, check, and rebound signs present; arm ataxia follows leg ataxia by months to years
  • Weakness and spasticity (LE >> UE); dysarthric speech (slow, progressively softer, may cause choking from uncoordinated respiratory muscles)
  • Areflexia (tendon reflexes abolished) with extensor plantar responses (Babinski) plus flexor spasms — an unusual, distinguishing combination
  • Loss of vibratory and position sense early; touch/pain sensation may diminish late
  • Optic atrophy, nystagmus, and hearing loss may occur; bladder dysfunction; personality changes (emotional lability)
Clinical overview — dysarthria, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, diabetes mellitus, kyphoscoliosis, areflexia, pallhypesthesia, ataxic gait, and pes cavus

Skeletal Findings

  • Pes cavus with hammer toes
  • Kyphoscoliosis
  • Talipes equinovarus

Systemic Findings

  • Cardiac disease in ~90%; cardiomegaly in >50%; concentric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (palpitations, arrhythmias, dyspnea, exercise intolerance)
  • Diabetes mellitus in ~10%; impaired glucose tolerance in another ~10%
Spine X-ray — severe scoliosis (95° curve), a common skeletal complication of Friedreich ataxia
Prognosis

Nonambulation is common by age 20–30. Most patients succumb to cardiomyopathy before age 35 (average age at death ~37 years) — heart failure from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the most common cause of death, followed by respiratory complications.

3 · Diagnostic Testing
Diagnostic Approach
  • Trinucleotide (GAA) repeat expansion assay — should be performed in all suspected cases; definitive diagnosis
  • Sensory nerve conduction studies: absent or reduced sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs); motor conduction remains normal until advanced stages
  • ECG: T-wave inversion, ventricular hypertrophy; echocardiography: symmetric, concentric ventricular hypertrophy; chest film for cardiopathy
  • MRI brain and spinal cord: cervical spinal cord atrophy/degeneration with a normal-sized cerebellum
Pearls

Areflexia plus an extensor plantar (Babinski) response together is an unusual combination — dorsal root ganglia loss abolishes the reflex arc while corticospinal tract degeneration produces the Babinski sign. Seeing both together should point specifically to Friedreich ataxia.

On MRI, Friedreich ataxia shows cervical cord atrophy with a normal-sized cerebellum — the opposite imaging pattern from the autosomal dominant SCAs, which typically show cerebellar atrophy instead.

🧠 Practice Questions — Friedreich Ataxia
LO 1–2 Dorsal columns + lateral corticospinal tract B12 (cobalamin) deficiency Treatable if caught early

🩹 Subacute Combined Degeneration

🎯 How boards would word it

A 67-year-old man presents with several months of progressive numbness and tingling in his feet, followed more recently by unsteady gait and leg stiffness. He reports fatigue and a strict vegan diet for the past 15 years. On exam he has loss of vibration and proprioception in both feet, hyperreflexia at the knees, bilateral Babinski signs, and a positive Romberg test. He also appears mildly pale with a smooth, red tongue. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A disease of the large myelinated sensory and motor systems of the peripheral nerves, spinal cord, and brain — degeneration occurs in the peripheral nerves, anterior and lateral columns, and the lateral corticospinal tract of the spinal cord, secondary to vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency. A treatable myelopathy if diagnosed early. Synonyms: SCD, vitamin B12 deficiency, posterolateral sclerosis.

  • Predominantly affects adults >40, with highest incidence age 50–80
  • B12 deficiency is the most common cause of SCD, but not all B12-deficient individuals develop SCD
  • B12 deficiency prevalence: 5–12% of the elderly population; among those with confirmed B12 deficiency, SCD incidence is ~14%
Etiology
  • B12 deficiency from failure to transfer minute amounts of the vitamin across the intestinal wall
  • Pernicious anemia — autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor — is a classic associated cause
  • Nitrous oxide exposure (recreational or anesthetic) inactivates B12 and can precipitate SCD
  • Vegan diets are low in B12; risk is greater in young children, pregnant women, and the elderly, and more common in developing regions due to malnutrition
  • Other risk factors: gastric abnormalities, small bowel disease, pancreatic disease, raw freshwater fish consumption, genetic abnormalities
  • Copper deficiency can mimic SCD almost exactly — worth checking if B12 is normal but the clinical picture fits
Pathophysiology
  • B12 deficiency → spongy vacuolation, intramyelinic and interstitial edema of myelin sheaths → eventual destruction and astrocytosis
  • B12 is required for the fatty acid synthesis pathway that produces and maintains myelin
  • Initially targets the heavily myelinated posterior and lateral columns; over time, both ascending sensory and descending motor tracts become demyelinated
  • Affects the dorsal column, spinocerebellar, and corticospinal systems of the spinal cord
Myelin stain (black = intact myelin) — thoracic (A) and lumbar (B) spinal cord sections; pale areas in the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tract indicate demyelination
2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Subacute, progressive, diffuse and symmetric: ataxia, numbness and tingling in the lower extremities, progressing to weakness, spasticity, increased reflexes, and a Babinski sign (upper motor neuron signs).

  • Begins bilaterally with posterior column signs — paresthesias, reduced touch/joint/pressure sensation — followed over several weeks by spastic weakness and eventually ataxic paraplegia
  • Insidious onset, often first noticed as paresthesias in the hands and feet
  • Loss of proprioception and vibratory sense; spasticity and ataxic weakness usually limited to the legs
  • Visual impairment from optic neuropathy (optic atrophy)
  • Frontal white matter cognitive symptoms — signs of (reversible) dementia, depression, or paranoia
  • Autonomic dysfunction: impotence, incontinence
Systemic Clues (Pernicious Anemia)

Depending on etiology, signs and symptoms of pernicious anemia may accompany the neurologic picture: fatigue, pallor, mild scleral icterus/jaundice, and glossitis.

Pearl

The "combined" in subacute combined degeneration refers to simultaneous dorsal column and lateral corticospinal tract involvement — sensory ataxia and vibration/proprioception loss plus spasticity, hyperreflexia, and a Babinski sign together in the same patient. (Note: coexisting peripheral neuropathy can sometimes blunt the expected hyperreflexia, so the exam picture can look mixed.)

Treatment Context

Beyond this LO's core scope: if treated early with prompt B12 supplementation, signs and symptoms may be reversible — but once complete paraplegia has developed, recovery is poor. This reversibility window is exactly why early recognition matters so much in SCD.
